title: SAUL WENT LOOKING FOR MISSING DONKEYS—AND CAME HOME ANOINTED AS ISRAEL’S KING
paragraphs:
SAUL WENT LOOKING FOR MISSING DONKEYS—AND CAME HOME ANOINTED AS ISRAEL’S KING
He thought he was searching for something his father had lost. He had no idea God was using the loss to lead him toward a calling he never went looking for.
Imagine leaving home in the morning looking for donkeys…
…and returning with the knowledge that you have been chosen to become king.
Not promoted.
Not noticed by an influential man.
Not handed a better job.
Anointed king of Israel.

That sounds almost absurd until you realize how often God has used ordinary frustrations, inconvenient detours, unanswered questions, closed doors, and seemingly meaningless losses to move people into places they never would have entered voluntarily.
And maybe that is why Saul’s story in 1 Samuel 9–10 feels strangely personal.
Because some of us are still staring at the missing donkeys.
We are frustrated about what disappeared.
Confused about what changed.
Exhausted from searching.
Wondering why God allowed something that seemed stable to suddenly become uncertain.
We keep asking, “Where did it go?”
While God may be doing something much deeper than returning what was lost.
The story begins without trumpets.
There is no throne.
No palace.
No royal procession.
There are missing animals.
Kish, Saul’s father, had lost some donkeys, and he told his son to take a servant and go search for them.
So Saul went.
That is important.
Before Saul ever carried the title of king, Scripture shows him carrying out an ordinary responsibility for his father.
He did not wake up chasing greatness.
He went looking for donkeys.
Through the hill country of Ephraim.
Through Shalishah.
Through Shaalim.
Through the territory of Benjamin.
Again and again…
nothing.
Imagine the frustration.
Another hill.
Another road.
Another village.
Another disappointment.
No donkeys.
Eventually Saul became concerned that his father would stop worrying about the animals and start worrying about him.
From Saul’s perspective, the mission was failing.
But from heaven’s perspective, the journey was approaching its appointed destination.
That distinction can change the way you understand some of the most confusing seasons of your life.
Something can look unsuccessful from where you are standing while still being used within the providence of God.
Saul could not see what the reader is allowed to see.
Before Saul arrives, God has already spoken to Samuel.
The Hebrew text of 1 Samuel 9:15 uses an intimate expression:
וַיהוָה גָּלָה אֶת־אֹזֶן שְׁמוּאֵל
VaYHWH galah et-ozen Shemu’el.
Literally, the LORD had “uncovered Samuel’s ear.”
In other words, God privately revealed to Samuel what was about to happen.
And what God told Samuel is astonishing.
Approximately a day before Saul arrived, the LORD told Samuel that a man from Benjamin would come to him and that Samuel was to anoint him as ruler over Israel.
Saul was searching.
Samuel was expecting.
Saul saw missing donkeys.
Samuel had received revelation.
Saul thought he was trying to solve a family problem.
God was moving the story toward an anointing.
Do not misunderstand this passage.
It does not teach that every inconvenience means God is secretly preparing you for fame, promotion, wealth, leadership, or some spectacular earthly breakthrough.
That is not the Gospel.
Sometimes a lost thing is simply lost.
Sometimes suffering remains painful.
Sometimes what disappears does not come back.
And Saul’s later life itself warns us against turning his anointing into a simplistic prosperity slogan.
But 1 Samuel 9 does show something beautiful about divine providence:
God can accomplish purposes people cannot yet see through circumstances that appear painfully ordinary.
That matters when your life does not make sense.
Because perhaps you have had your own “missing donkeys.”
The relationship you thought would last.
The opportunity you were sure was yours.
The plan that collapsed.
The prayer that did not unfold the way you expected.
The season that has gone on longer than you imagined.
The door that closed without explanation.
The thing you have been desperately trying to recover.
And you keep thinking:
“If I could just get this back, everything would be okay.”
Saul probably wanted something similarly simple.
Find the animals.
Return home.
Mission accomplished.
But then his servant suggested they visit the man of God.
One apparently small suggestion changed the direction of the journey.
And when Saul finally met Samuel, Samuel said something Saul could never have expected.
Do not worry about the donkeys.
They had been found.
Think about that.
The problem Saul had been chasing was already being resolved while Saul was being led toward something he did not know existed.
Then Samuel spoke words that must have stopped him cold.
He pointed toward Saul and his father’s household in connection with “all the desire of Israel.”
Saul’s response reveals how unlikely this must have sounded to him.
He essentially asked:
Why me?
He was from Benjamin—the smallest tribe of Israel—and from a comparatively insignificant family within Benjamin.
Whether Saul’s words reflected genuine humility, social convention, or something more complicated, the shock in the scene is unmistakable.
He came asking about donkeys.
Samuel began speaking about Israel.
He came carrying the concerns of his father’s house.
Suddenly he was being confronted with a calling involving an entire nation.
Then Samuel took a flask of oil.
And poured it over Saul’s head.
The Hebrew of 1 Samuel 10:1 says:
וַיִּקַּח שְׁמוּאֵל אֶת־פַּךְ הַשֶּׁמֶן וַיִּצֹק עַל־רֹאשׁוֹ
Vayyiqqach Shemu’el et-pakh hashemen, vayitzok al-rosho.
Samuel took the flask of oil…
and poured it upon Saul’s head.
The ordinary search had arrived at an extraordinary moment.
Oil running down his head.
Samuel kissing him.
Words of divine appointment ringing in his ears.
The man who had walked into the region looking for his father’s animals was being anointed as ruler over the LORD’s inheritance.
And then God gave him confirming signs.
He would meet men who would tell him the donkeys had been found.
He would encounter others carrying goats, bread, and wine.
He would meet a company of prophets.
And something would happen inside Saul himself.
One of the most striking statements appears in 1 Samuel 10:6:
וְצָלְחָה עָלֶיךָ רוּחַ יְהוָה
Vetzalchah alekha Ruach YHWH.
“The Spirit of the LORD will rush upon you.”
Samuel continued:
וְנֶהְפַּכְתָּ לְאִישׁ אַחֵר
Venehpákhta le’ish acher.
“You shall be turned into another man.”
And shortly afterward Scripture says:
וַיַּהֲפָךְ־לוֹ אֱלֹהִים לֵב אַחֵר
Vayyahafoḵ-lo Elohim lev acher.
“God changed for him another heart,” or more naturally, “God gave him another heart.”
There is something breathtaking about that moment.
But there is also something sobering about it.
Because if you know the rest of Saul’s story, you know that an extraordinary beginning did not guarantee an extraordinary ending.
Saul was genuinely chosen.
Genuinely anointed.
Genuinely empowered for the role God had given him.
And yet Saul would later disobey.
He would become increasingly consumed with preserving his position.
Fear would distort him.
Jealousy would poison him.
David would become a threat in Saul’s eyes.
The man who once seemed small in his own estimation would eventually fight desperately to hold onto a throne God had told him he would lose.
And this is where the story stops being merely inspirational.
This is where it becomes a warning.
Because finding your calling is not the same thing as faithfully walking with God.
Being used by God is not permission to stop obeying God.
Yesterday’s anointing cannot become tomorrow’s excuse for rebellion.
A powerful beginning cannot substitute for continuing faithfulness.
You can receive responsibility and still mishandle it.
You can experience the mercy of God and still need daily surrender.
You can be surrounded by religious activity while your heart quietly begins protecting an idol.
For Saul, eventually, the throne became something he was desperate to preserve.
And before we condemn him too quickly, we should ask what throne we are protecting.
Reputation?
Approval?
Control?
Money?
Influence?
A relationship?
An image?
A ministry?
The need to always appear strong?
What do you become defensive about when obedience to God threatens it?
That question hurts.
It is supposed to.
Because Scripture was not given merely so we could stand safely outside its stories and criticize everyone who failed.
The Word exposes us.
Saul’s tragedy whispers a warning across the centuries:
You can be close to holy things while still resisting the Holy One.
You can know that God has called you to obedience and still negotiate with Him.
You can begin with humility and slowly become addicted to protecting yourself.
And perhaps the saddest irony is that Saul went looking for animals that belonged to his father…
then spent years trying to hold onto a kingdom that ultimately belonged to God.
That is what sin does.
It convinces us to clutch what was never truly ours.
But this story belongs inside a much larger biblical story.
Because Saul was not Israel’s ultimate king.
Neither was David.
Israel’s kings, even the greatest of them, pointed beyond themselves toward the need for a King who would not collapse beneath the weight of human sin.
And eventually another King came.
Jesus Christ.
He did not need Samuel’s flask of oil to establish His identity.
He is the Messiah—the Christ.
Both titles carry the idea of the Anointed One.
The Hebrew מָשִׁיחַ, mashiach.
The Greek Χριστός, Christos.
Jesus is the true and greater King.
Saul received a kingdom and eventually grasped to preserve it.
Jesus possessed divine glory and humbled Himself.
Saul’s fear drove him toward destructive self-preservation.
Jesus willingly walked toward the cross.
Saul pursued David, seeking his death.
Jesus pursued sinners knowing His pursuit would lead to His own death.
Saul's kingdom fractured.
Christ’s kingdom will never end.
And here is where your story enters the Gospel.
You may have come here because the title sounded strange.
Missing donkeys.
A future king.
An unbelievable detour.
But perhaps underneath everything else, you are searching too.
Maybe you are searching for peace.
For identity.
For forgiveness.
For something that will finally silence the shame.
Maybe you have spent years trying to recover a version of yourself you lost somewhere along the way.
Maybe nobody knows what you did.
Or what was done to you.
Maybe you can smile convincingly.
Post beautifully.
Attend church.
Quote Scripture.
Say, “God is good.”
And still lie awake at night wondering whether Jesus could possibly want the person behind the presentation.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel is not that God discovered you were secretly good.
The Gospel is that while we were sinners, Christ died for us.
You do not have to manufacture innocence before approaching Jesus.
You come guilty.
He offers grace.
You come stained.
He cleanses.
You come unable to purchase your redemption.
Christ has paid the price.
You come carrying sin that must be confessed and forsaken.
He does not call you to hide it more successfully.
He calls you to repent and believe.
That is why the Gospel is scandalous grace.
Not cheap grace.
Not grace that pretends sin does not matter.
Grace purchased at the cross, where we discover exactly how serious sin is—and exactly how far the love of God went to rescue sinners.
Jesus does not merely improve the public version of you.
He calls the real you.
The ashamed you.
The angry you.
The addicted you.
The exhausted you.
The secretly jealous you.
The religious you.
The wandering you.
The person underneath all the defenses.
And He calls you not merely into a better mood but into repentance, faith, forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and a transformed life under His lordship.
Maybe your greatest problem is not the “missing donkey” you have been begging God to return.
Maybe your greatest need is the King.
Jesus.
Because you can recover what you lost and still lose your soul.
You can get the relationship back.
Get the money.
Get the opportunity.
Get the recognition.
Get the answer you wanted.
And still remain separated from God.
But if you have Christ, then even when earthly circumstances remain painful, you possess something suffering cannot ultimately steal.
Forgiveness.
Adoption.
Hope.
Eternal life.
A Savior who entered death and walked out of the grave.
This is where Saul’s story leaves us trembling.
He found the donkeys.
He received the crown.
Yet the crown could not save his heart.
And neither can whatever you are chasing save yours.
Only Christ can.
So stop hiding behind religion.
Stop promising God that someday you will surrender.
Stop treating repentance as something you will do when life becomes convenient.
If the Spirit of God is exposing something while you read this, bring it into the light.
Confess it.
Turn from it.
Run to Christ.
There is mercy for repentant sinners.
There is forgiveness at the cross.
There is no sin you can cleanse by pretending it never happened.
But there is cleansing in Jesus Christ for those who come to Him.
And if this exposed something you have been hiding, be honest.
Your comment may become the sentence another wounded believer needed to see to realize they are not the only one struggling.
Then think of one person who needs this story.
Not someone you want to embarrass.
Someone you love.
If the Gospel has given you something worth sharing, let your sharing become one simple way of making that truth visible.
Because one day you may become so focused on what disappeared that you need to remember Saul walking mile after mile searching for donkeys, unaware of what awaited him.

But if this ministry genuinely helps you grow in Christ and you want to help us reach more people with the Gospel, you can glorify God through generous, willing stewardship—including supporting Gospel work and sharing biblical truth with others.
Gospel Warrior cannot save you.
A Christian book cannot save you.
A church membership cannot save you.
Your generosity cannot save you.
Your good works cannot save you.
Jesus saves.
Everything else must remain beneath Him.
So share because the Gospel is worth sharing.
Support Gospel work because you genuinely want others to hear.
Give freely, not under compulsion.
Follow because you want to stay close to biblical truth.
Save what helps you remember Christ.
And through all of it…
worship Jesus.
Because perhaps the most haunting lesson from Saul is not that an ordinary man once went searching for missing donkeys and came home anointed to be king.
It is that a person can receive something extraordinary from God and still eventually lose sight of God Himself.
Do not make that mistake.
Do not become so obsessed with finding what you lost that you miss what God is revealing through His Word.
Do not become so fascinated with your calling that you neglect the One who called you.
Do not become so protective of your little kingdom that you resist the true King.
And do not allow shame to convince you that your worst chapter must become the final chapter.
Peter failed.
Thomas doubted.
Paul persecuted the church before Christ confronted him.
Sinners have fallen at the feet of Jesus for centuries and discovered that His grace is greater than the identities their sins had written over them.
The cross still stands.
The tomb is still empty.
Christ still saves.
Repentance is still possible.
Grace is still offered.
And Jesus is still rewriting stories.
Maybe you started reading because a man went looking for donkeys.
Maybe you reached the end because somewhere between Saul’s search and Saul’s anointing, God’s Word started searching you.
So here is the line I hope follows you long after you close this page:
You may spend half your life searching for what went missing, only to discover that your deepest need was never the thing you lost—it was the King who came looking for you.
